newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thailand wrestles with domestic economic woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thailand wrestles with domestic economic woes.

text.p: Thailand's domestic economic woes look set to deepen, economists and analysts warned on Thursday, despite data showing an improvement in its external sector.

Authorities needed to ease tight monetary policy, otherwise interest rates at around 13.25 percent, among the region's highest, could exacerbate problems, the analysts said. The high rates have been blamed for denting consumer spending and slowing maufacturing activity.

The bright spots in a string of key monthly indicators released by the central bank on Thursday were a current account deficit which narrowed to a two-and-a-half-year low in February, and a shrinking trade deficit in the same month.
But a closer look at the numbers showed the economic picture was less than rosy.
The narrower February trade deficit at 21.7 billion baht ($835 million) versus 39.0 billion in January was due to a big downturn in imports and not export growth, analysts said.

Other data released by the central bank pointed to a sluggish economy. Private investment growth for February fell to 6.3 percent from 6.8 percent year-on-year. The manufacturing production index slid to 2.4 percent in February from 4.2 percent in January.
Analysts said the overall Thai economic picture was not encouraging although the government was aiming for 6.8 percent growth this year. Many analysts see growth below six percent.

Thailand is grappling with many economic problems such as high interest rates, a battered stock market, a cash-strapped and depressed property sector and a financial sector reeling from billions of dollars in bad loans to mainly property firms.

"Supplies in the property market do not go hand in hand with an economy that is slowing. It takes one or the other. The interest rate must come down now or problems will escalate," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett Asia.

"Thailand's (minimum lending rate) is stubbornly stuck at 13.0-13.50 percent while exports have shrunk sharply. If this trend continues, the private investment index and the manufucturing production index will move into negative territory very soon," he added.
Thailand maintains high interest rates to defend the baht from speculative attacks. The high rates are also aimed at curbing domestic demand and helping narrow the current account and trade deficits.
With the lid placed on domestic demand, Thailand will have to rely heavily on exports to spur growth, analysts said.
"Domestic demand will not pick up if Thai authorities keep interest rates this high," said Warut Sivasariyanon, acting head of resarch at ING Barings.

But exports figures posted in February were disappointing. Exports growth contracted 5.5 percent year-on-year in that month, leaving economists to question whether there would be a healthy turnaround in the sector this year.
Bank of Thailand chief economist Kleothong Hetrakul saw some improvement for exports in March. However, Singapore-based research house I.D.E.A. said a recovery was still months away.
"A drop in imports is normally due to a decrease in raw material and capital goods purchases. The sharp drop thus indicates that an export recovery will be yet some months away," it said in a report.
Other analysts said the improving external balance picture could give Thai authorities room to cut interest rates to fire up the economy.
Kleothong said rates could come down only if the forex market was not too volatile and interbank rates stabilised.
